name: Refeed days / diet breaks
lead: Refeed days and diet breaks are planned periods of higher energy intake, usually extra carbohydrate, placed inside a longer calorie-restricted diet. A refeed lasts a day or two; a diet break lasts longer, such as a week at maintenance intake. People use them while cutting body fat for a leaner, more defined physique, with the aim of keeping training quality and muscle while the scale comes down.[1][2]

Proponents describe several benefits: easier adherence, better gym performance, and less of the slowdown in energy expenditure that follows weight loss. Reviews describe this slowdown as metabolic adaptation, and list programmed refeeds and diet breaks among strategies discussed to counter it.[3][1] There is also a plain physiological effect: glycogen is stored with water, so carbohydrate-rich days restore glycogen and can add scale weight and muscle fullness.[4][5]

Research is growing. A 2025 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials (881 participants) found intermittent dieting with breaks and continuous restriction improved body composition similarly, with a smaller drop in resting metabolic rate with breaks.[6] A small 2026 trial in women with obesity reached comparable fat loss in both patterns.[7]

chain: Planned higher-calorie days or weeks interrupt a calorie deficit

angle.text: Refeeds and diet breaks are a way of making a cut easier to sustain so that fat loss continues while muscle and training quality are protected. Physique competitors and gym dieters use them to reach a leaner, fuller-looking physique; the glycogen they restore also gives a fuller muscle appearance.

paras: A refeed raises calories for a short stretch, usually through carbohydrate, while a diet break pauses the deficit for a longer stretch. Both are forms of intermittent energy restriction, in which restriction alternates with periods of greater intake.[1] They are related to carbohydrate loading and carb cycling, in which carbohydrate intake is deliberately varied.[5]

A review of nutrition for physique athletes notes that slower rates of weight loss are preferable for attenuating the loss of fat-free mass, and that intermittent strategies such as diet breaks and refeeds are possibly beneficial.[2]

Weight loss is followed by metabolic adaptation, in which the body works to regain the mass it lost. Reviews list increasing protein, choosing high-fiber foods, and programming refeeds and diet breaks among strategies discussed against it.[3]

Glycogen is stored hydrated with about three to four parts water per part glycogen, so a carbohydrate-rich refeed can restore glycogen and add water weight.[4] Carbohydrate loading in endurance sport is documented to cause water retention and weight gain of this kind.[5] The athlete review notes that intermittent periods of energy balance may attenuate some adaptive responses, though evidence in athletes is limited.[1]

A systematic review and meta-analysis in Nutrition Reviews (2025) pooled 12 randomized trials with 881 participants. Both intermittent dieting with breaks and continuous energy restriction improved body mass, fat mass, BMI, body fat percentage and waist circumference, with no significant group differences; resting metabolic rate fell significantly only with continuous restriction. The authors concluded that breaks are a viable strategy for improving body composition and reducing metabolic adaptation.[6]

A 2021 secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial followed 26 resistance-trained athletes after 12 weeks of intermittent restriction. A one-week diet break at maintenance intake raised body weight by 0.6 kg and fat-free mass by 0.7 kg with no significant change in fat mass, and leg muscle endurance improved.[8]

A 2026 randomized trial in 30 women with obesity compared 12 weeks of continuous restriction with refeeds and planned breaks at a 25 percent deficit. Fat mass fell by about 9 kg in both groups, with a nonsignificant trend toward more fat-free mass in the refeed group; the authors called for larger trials.[7]

T Nation log threads show a range of attitudes. One user notes that the first question people ask when someone starts a cut is when the first cheat meal or refeed will be, another reports using targeted keto with refeed days and staying lean without heavy hunger, and a third says they lost weight without ever using refeeds and wondered if they missed an option.[11][10][9]

lore.intro: In bodybuilding and strength forums, refeeds and cheat meals are a standard part of cutting talk, described as a performance and sanity aid.[9][10][11]

claims.claim: Refeeds keep metabolism and hunger in check during a cut
claims.believers: A T Nation member says refeed days let him eat a lot and stay lean without constant hunger.[10]
claims.experts: Reviews describe metabolic adaptation to weight loss and list refeeds among strategies discussed. A 2025 meta-analysis found a smaller drop in resting metabolic rate with diet breaks.[3][6]

claims.claim: A refeed adds fullness to muscles
claims.believers: Dieters describe a fuller look after carbohydrate days.[10]
claims.experts: Glycogen is stored with water, so carbohydrate intake changes can shift weight in the short term.[4]

claims.claim: Diet breaks lead to more fat loss than steady dieting
claims.believers: Proponents say breaks make a diet more effective, and forum members ask early on when the first refeed is.[11]
claims.experts: A meta-analysis and a 2026 trial found similar fat loss with and without breaks.[6][7]

quick.overview:
Refeed days and diet breaks are planned periods of increased food intake, often extra carbohydrate, inserted into a calorie-restricted diet. People who diet for a lean look use them in the belief that they aid adherence, training and fullness of the muscles.

Because carbohydrate is stored with water, a refeed can raise scale weight and change how full or flat the physique looks.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute benefits to restoring glycogen and moderating hunger and hormonal responses to dieting. Glycogen is stored with roughly three to four parts water, which accounts for short-term weight changes.
quick.risks: Documented risks are mainly practical, such as stalling the calorie deficit or triggering overeating. People with eating disorders are generally advised against rigid diet cycles.
